one_liner: Repeated soiling of underwear or other places by a child aged four or older, usually from constipation.
in_simple_words: Encopresis is when a child aged four or older repeatedly passes stool into their clothes or in inappropriate places, at least once a month for three months, and it isn't caused by a medical condition. It usually comes from long-standing constipation: a hard mass builds up, the bowel stretches, and softer stool leaks around it without the child feeling it. Children don't do this on purpose. Treating the constipation, with routine and patience, usually fixes it.
what_it_can_feel_like: We thought he was being defiant. The paediatrician explained his bowel was so stretched he genuinely couldn't feel it. I felt awful for the shouting.
The hardest part was school. Once the nurse knew, she helped him clean up quietly and nobody else needed to know.
common_signs: Repeated soiling of clothes or inappropriate places, at age four or older
At least once a month for three months
Usually signs of constipation: hard or very large stools, tummy pain, avoiding the toilet
Child may not notice the smell or feel it happening
Shame, hiding soiled clothes, teasing at school

myths_vs_facts.fact: In most cases the child can't feel the leak because a stretched bowel has lost sensation. It's a physical problem with a physical fix.

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's about toilet training being done wrong.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Constipation, painful stools, illness, diet, and fear of the toilet are the usual roots. Parents can help now, whatever happened before.
Doctors routinely prescribe and monitor child-safe laxatives to clear the build-up and keep stools soft while the bowel recovers. Stopping too early is the common mistake.

how_common.plain: About 1 in 100 five-year-olds have encopresis, more boys than girls. It becomes less common with age.
how_common.figure: About 1% of 5-year-olds (DSM-5-TR text); estimates in studies range roughly 0.8%–7.8%

what_helps.plain_summary: The main treatment is medical: a doctor clears the built-up stool with laxatives, then keeps stools soft for months with a maintenance dose, prescribed and monitored, while the bowel shrinks back and sensation returns. Alongside that, a regular toilet routine (sitting after meals, feet supported, no pressure), a diet with enough fibre and fluids, and calm praise for sitting rather than for results. Behavioural support helps children who have become afraid of the toilet. If there's no constipation, a different assessment is needed.
evidence_based_options: Disimpaction and maintenance laxatives prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Scheduled toilet sitting after meals with a footstool
Behavioural support for toilet fear or refusal; family education
self_help_that_supports_care: No blame, no punishment; matter-of-fact clean-up kits at home and school
A sticker chart for sitting on the toilet, not for staying clean
Keeping going with the laxatives for as long as the doctor advises
A quiet word with the school so the child isn't shamed

when_to_reach_out: If a child aged four or older is regularly soiling, see a doctor. Treating constipation early is easier and kinder. See a doctor urgently if there's severe tummy pain, vomiting, or blood.
is_not: Accidents during toilet training, a single bout of diarrhoea, or soiling caused by a bowel condition, nerve problem, or medication are not encopresis.
hope_note: With the right treatment the bowel recovers, sensation returns, and the soiling stops. Children and families get their confidence back.
